doc.title: Arturo Sandoval interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2023

title: Playing fast is not throwing notes; do not copy others
summary: He defends fast playing, names Brecker, Peterson and Pedersen as heroes, says playing a bad copy is foolish, and demonstrates that he knows each note.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: you know. And the way to gather your ideas that makes sense. I have some melodic — some people for example, they believe when you’re playing fast you are throwing notes. That’s a stupid mistake. We don’t throw in notes. For something, and the way we learn solfeggio, we name it, every name of the notes. We don’t say do-re-me da-ba-da — no no. We say do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do [continues to scat quickly]. When I’m playing fast, very fast, some people criticize, yeah okay. And I always, my response to that is I would love to play the trumpet in the way Michael Brecker played the tenor or Oscar Peterson played the piano. That’s my goal, my heroes, the people who are or on their way — Neils-Henning Orsted Pederson plays the acoustic bass. He is my hero in terms of the bass. My hero. And some people want you to play just for example imitating other great musicians. If you put a mute on they want you sound like Miles. If you sound different they don’t give credit and they don’t really appreciate it. I say man, to be a copy of the original is the most stupid thing.

To copy, to be a bad copy of the original is a very stupid idea. Our goal should be to express ourselves in the way you feel. In the way, you know, and also modesty apart, if you have been practicing for so many years, for so millions of hours, it’s to develop skill. To do what? Because there’s two ways when you’re a professional musician. You play what you want, or you play what you can. I swear, I want to belong to the first group. I want to play in the way I want. You could do that. What you have to do: control your instrument, be in control. Spend millions of hours practicing to develop the skill and to have that preparation to play your instrument in the way you feel and the way you want, without struggling with frustration and limitations. Some people don’t get it. If I play something, for example “If I Do”
I am completely conscious of what I was doing. I wasn’t throwing notes. No. I know the name of every note, and I know the reason of every note. Why I play.
Why you play it. Because were you —
Because it’s a kind of line, melodical. It’s a kind of line that I like it because it’s in the tradition of bebop or jazz in general, and also I know those notes belong and work well with the chord.
